facts: Two figures are **similar** when their matching angles are equal, and their matching sides are then all in the same ratio.
Any two right-angled triangles containing the same angle $\theta$ are similar, because their angles match: $90^{\circ}$, $\theta$, and $180^{\circ}-90^{\circ}-\theta$.
Enlarging by a scale factor $k$ multiplies **both** lengths in a ratio by $k$, and the factor cancels: $\dfrac{kb}{kc}=\dfrac{b}{c}$.
So $\sin\theta$, $\cos\theta$ and $\tan\theta$ depend **only on the angle** $\theta$, never on how big the triangle is.
Change the **size** of the triangle and the ratios stay the same; change the **angle** and the ratios change.
The hypotenuse is the longest side, so $\sin\theta$ and $\cos\theta$ are always between $0$ and $1$.

foundation.solution_text:
Triangle $A$:
$\sin\theta=\dfrac{\text{Opp}}{\text{Hyp}}=\dfrac{3}{5}$
Triangle $B$:
$\sin\theta=\dfrac{\text{Opp}}{\text{Hyp}}=\dfrac{6}{10}=\dfrac{3}{5}$
The sine ratio is the same in both triangles.

Triangle $A$:
$\cos\theta=\dfrac{\text{Adj}}{\text{Hyp}}=\dfrac{6}{10}=\dfrac{3}{5}$
Triangle $B$:
$\cos\theta=\dfrac{\text{Adj}}{\text{Hyp}}=\dfrac{9}{15}=\dfrac{3}{5}$
The cosine ratio is the same in both triangles.

Triangle $A$:
$\tan\theta=\dfrac{\text{Opp}}{\text{Adj}}=\dfrac{6}{8}=\dfrac{3}{4}$
Triangle $B$:
$\tan\theta=\dfrac{\text{Opp}}{\text{Adj}}=\dfrac{3}{4}$
Making the triangle smaller does not change the tangent ratio.

Each triangle has angles $90^{\circ}$, $\theta$ and $180^{\circ}-90^{\circ}-\theta$, so the two triangles are similar.
Every side of $B$ is twice the matching side of $A$, so the factor of $2$ cancels in the ratio:
$\cos\theta=\dfrac{6}{16}=\dfrac{3}{8}$, the same as $\dfrac{3}{8}$ in triangle $A$.

Triangle $A$: $\dfrac{4}{8}=\dfrac{1}{2}$
Triangle $B$: $\dfrac{3.5}{7}=\dfrac{1}{2}$
Triangle $C$: $\dfrac{5}{10}=\dfrac{1}{2}$
All three give $\dfrac{1}{2}$, because every right-angled triangle containing $60^{\circ}$ is similar.

(i) The sides become $48\text{ cm}$, $20\text{ cm}$ and $52\text{ cm}$.
(ii) $\theta$ does not change, because an enlargement keeps all angles equal.
(iii) $\sin\theta=\dfrac{20}{52}=\dfrac{5}{13}$, the same as $\dfrac{5}{13}$ before the enlargement.

New sides: $28\text{ cm}$, $21\text{ cm}$ and $35\text{ cm}$.
$\sin\theta=\dfrac{21}{35}$
$=\dfrac{3}{5}$

Triangle $A$: $\dfrac{3}{6}=\dfrac{1}{2}$
Triangle $B$: $\dfrac{4}{9}$
Triangle $C$: $\dfrac{4}{10}=\dfrac{2}{5}$
Only triangle $A$ gives $\dfrac{1}{2}$, so $\theta=60^{\circ}$ in triangle $A$.

Both simplify to $\dfrac{4}{5}$, so reducing the triangle leaves the sine ratio unchanged.

Triangle $C$: $\tan\theta=\dfrac{9}{6}=\dfrac{3}{2}$
The tangent ratio is fixed by the angle $\theta$, not by the size of the triangle.

Triangle $A$: $\tan\theta=\dfrac{2}{4}=0.5$
Triangle $B$: $\tan\theta=\dfrac{3}{5}=0.6$
Triangle $C$: $\tan\theta=\dfrac{3}{6}=0.5$
Triangles $A$ and $C$ contain the angle; they are similar to each other, but $B$ is not.

$\cos\phi=\dfrac{6}{10}=\dfrac{3}{5}$
They are not equal. The triangles are the same size, but $\theta$ and $\phi$ are different angles, so the ratio is decided by the angle and not by the size.

Triangle $A$:

Triangle $B$:

The scale factor $3$ cancels, so the tangent ratio is unchanged.

development.question_text:
A right-angled triangle has $\cos\theta=\dfrac{7}{25}$.
Every side is multiplied by $0.4$.
Write $\cos\theta$ for the new triangle and explain your answer.
development.solution_text:
$\cos\theta=\dfrac{0.4\times 7}{0.4\times 25}$
$=\dfrac{2.8}{10}$
$=\dfrac{7}{25}$
Both the adjacent side and the hypotenuse are multiplied by $0.4$, so the factor cancels and the ratio is unchanged.

mastery.question_text:
In every right-angled triangle containing a $45^{\circ}$ angle, $\tan 45^{\circ}=1$.
Use this to explain why every such triangle is isosceles.
mastery.solution_text:
$\tan 45^{\circ}=\dfrac{\text{Opp}}{\text{Adj}}=1$
so $\text{Opp}=\text{Adj}$.
The two shorter sides are equal in every right-angled triangle containing $45^{\circ}$, so every one of them is isosceles.

mastery.question_text: Explain why no right-angled triangle can have $\sin\theta=1.2$.
mastery.solution_text:
$\sin\theta=\dfrac{\text{Opp}}{\text{Hyp}}=1.2$ would need $\text{Opp}=1.2\times\text{Hyp}$.
That makes the opposite side longer than the hypotenuse, but the hypotenuse is always the longest side of a right-angled triangle.
No such triangle exists, so $\sin\theta$ can never be greater than $1$.
